Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.11730.question: For the LLaMA 124M–500M experiments, how were validation loss and training compute matched between spectral and standard weight decay, which SVD-LLM compression baselines were compared, and what were the measured compression ratios and inference speedups?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

SliceGPT removes rows and columns after a principal-component transformation [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] . ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] and SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] use activation statistics to improve the factorization. Dobi-SVD learns layerwise truncation and reconstructs weights from truncated activations [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . Prehab fine-tunes a trained model for SVD compression [ Qin et al., 2025 ] . Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with Prehab in this setting. Our main experiments apply it throughout pretraining and evaluate compression and inference with SVD-LLM. Appendix B.4 compares post-training compression methods. Section 3 shows the resulting compression and inference gains.

Spectral weight decay lowers the effective rank of weight matrices, making them amenable to low-rank compression. We use SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , which gives the lowest validation loss in our matched comparison. We compress each weight matrix to its own effective rank, which varies substantially across layers (Figure 2 , middle). We leave the token embeddings and output head uncompressed because their ranks respond little to spectral weight decay, and compressing them even to their effective ranks sharply degrades model quality. The comparison and compression procedure are described in Appendix B.4 . Figure 3 (top) reports the maximum compression rate supported by each validation-loss distortion budget. Spectral weight decay substantially shifts this frontier upward at all three model scales. For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. The same factorization reduces the FLOPs of a linear layer when r ⁡ ( m + n ) < m ​ n r(m+n)<mn . This reduction does not translate directly into lower latency because the factorized forward pass evaluates ( U r ​ Σ r ) ​ ( V r ⊤ ​ X ) (U_{r}\Sigma_{r})(V_{r}^{\top}X) with two GEMMs instead of the single GEMM W ​ X WX . The additional kernel launch and intermediate activation can offset the reduction in FLOPs. To improve tensor-core utilization, we round the effective rank down to the nearest multiple of 16 16 , r l = max ⁡ ( 16 , 16 ​ ⌊ erank ⁡ ( W l ) 16 ⌋ ) , r_{l}=\max\!\left(16,\,16\left\lfloor\frac{\operatorname{erank}(W_{l})}{16}\right\rfloor\right), (3)

Adjusting an aligned rank by one step, ± 16 \pm 16 , has negligible effect on validation loss. We therefore use this rank-aligned compression scheme throughout. The factorized models outperform their dense counterparts only at large batch sizes, so we measure forward-pass latency with a batch size of 256 256 on a single GPU. For the 500 500 M model, spectral weight decay yields a 1.09 × 1.09\times speedup near a 2 % 2\% distortion budget and reaches 1.18 × 1.18\times at 4 % 4\% , compared with 1.01 × 1.01\times under standard weight decay (Figure 3 , bottom).

inspect:2610.10965.question: In the NanoGPT speedruns, how does Spectrally Targeted Muon compare with full Muon and other optimizer baselines on validation loss and training cost? Which singular-value directions are targeted, and how do the measured weight effective ranks change?

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

The Muon optimizer for deep learning works by orthogonalizing the update matrix ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) . Unlike many other proposed optimizers, this has been highly successful empirically for training large language models, especially when coupled with weight decay ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . This is because the matrix can be orthogonalized relatively efficiently, using methods such as Newton-Schulz or Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . The orthogonalization step can be thought of as applying the matrix sign function to the gradient matrix, which normalizes all the singular values to one, prompting the question of whether Muon’s success comes from amplifying small but important directions with small singular values ignored by standard gradient descent, or from normalizing large, degenerate directions with large singular values that misdirect the training. In this paper, we will explore a method to target this orthogonalization to singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ \tau , and we will also experiment with different values for this threshold, thus allowing us to interpolate between SGD and Muon with a spectrally targeted version. Specifically, we will apply these Muon variants to the two speedrun tasks originally used to show Muon’s performance, the CIFAR-10 dataset with a convolutional network, and the NanoGPT large language model, just as in Jordan et al. (2024b) . In addition to standard performance metrics, we will examine other metrics more pertinent to the linear-algebraic structure of our weight and update matrices. The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. The independent searches select 1.3 × 10 − 3 1.3\times 10^{-3} , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Adam, Muon, Pion, and ORCA, with final validation losses of 2.8824 2.8824 , 2.8460 2.8460 , 2.9790 2.9790 , and 2.8106 2.8106 , respectively; ORCA thus lowers the loss by a further 0.0354 0.0354 relative to the best Muon and stays within 0.002 0.002 of its own optimum across 1.6 × 10 − 3 1.6\times 10^{-3} to 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , showing that the improvement does not rely on a narrow learning-rate choice. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. Due to computational budget constraints, we focus our comparison on Muon and ORCA. matches.title: Lightweight and Versatile Learned Optimization by Recombination of Gradient History
matches.abstract_excerpt: This paper presents a lightweight and versatile learned optimizer that dynamically recombines gradient history, represented as averages over disjoint time spans. The optimizer reduces the prediction space to one scalar coefficient per gradient average, shared by multiple parameters. Progressively averaging older gradients minimizes memory cost of long history, while keeping their contributions independently accessible. A 37k-parameter network trained in 0.87 GPU-hours generalizes zero-shot to unseen tasks, lowering validation loss by 9.1% and 0.4% on BERT-Tiny and GPT-Tiny, and improving test accuracy over Adam by 3.5 %p on a Vision Transformer and by 2.7 %p on average across nine graph models, with FLOPs overhead as low as 0.3%.

assessment.label: relevant
assessment.reason: Proposes a memory-conscious optimizer and tests transfer to small language models.
assessment.evidence_quote: Progressively averaging older gradients minimizes memory cost of long history, while keeping their contributions independently accessible.

matches.title: Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights
matches.abstract_excerpt: Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional $\ell_2$ weight decay near rank deficiency. At $500$M and a $4\%$ distortion budget, it reaches $1.89\times$ compression and $1.18\times$ GPU inference speedup, compared with $1.14\times$ and $1.01\times$ after standard weight decay. matches.title: LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches
matches.abstract_excerpt: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. matches.title: ORCA: The Annealed Spectral Conditioning Optimizer for Faster, Better LLM Training
matches.abstract_excerpt: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. passages.text: Recent progress of foundation models with deep neural networks, such as large vision and large language models, has been remarkable [ 39 , 17 , 10 , 61 , 2 ] . When transferring these pre-trained models to a specific downstream task, one popular technique is full fine-tuning that updates all the model parameters. However, full fine-tuning of large foundation models is impractical due to their large number of parameters, requiring high computational and storage costs for each task-specific model. To address this issue, parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques have become a promising alternative to full fine-tuning [ 25 , 44 , 21 , 22 , 18 ] . Among these techniques, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto standard thanks to its simplicity and effectiveness [ 21 ] . Let W 0 , W ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0},W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} denote the weight matrices of a layer in the pre-trained and fine-tuned models, respectively. In LoRA, the weight update of full fine-tuning Δ ​ W ∈ ℝ m × n \Delta W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} from W 0 W_{0} to W W is approximated by low-rank matrix factorization 1 1 1 We here omit the scaling B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} by s ∈ ℝ s\in\mathbb{R} for simplicity as it can be merged into B B and A A [ 24 ] . as follows: W = W 0 + Δ ​ W ≈ W 0 + B ​ A ⊤ , \displaystyle W=W_{0}+\Delta W\approx W_{0}+BA^{\top}, (2) where B ∈ ℝ m × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} and A ∈ ℝ n × r A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} are trainable factors. Let ℒ : ℝ m × n → ℝ \mathcal{L}:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} denote the loss function for a downstream task. Then, LoRA is formulated as min ( B , A ) ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ ℒ ⁡ ( W 0 + B ​ A ⊤ ) , \min_{(B,A)\in\mathcal{X}}\mathcal{L}\left(W_{0}+BA^{\top}\right), (3)

where 𝒳 ≔ ℝ m × r × ℝ n × r \mathcal{X}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} denotes the original search space for this problem. By choosing a sufficiently small r ≪ min ⁡ ( m , n ) r\ll\min(m,n) , LoRA yields fewer trainable parameters and lower computational and storage costs than full fine-tuning, i.e., min W ∈ ℝ m × n ⁡ ℒ ⁡ ( W ) \min_{W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}}\mathcal{L}\left(W\right) .

LoRA was initially formulated by Hu et al. [21] and achieves comparable full fine-tuning performance despite having very few trainable parameters. However, it often exhibits a performance gap compared to full fine-tuning. We here summarize several studies to improve the performance of LoRA. Modeling (Architecture). Beyond the standard two-factor factorization [ 21 , 41 , 36 , 24 ] as described in 2 , three-factor factorization has been proposed recently [ 58 , 26 , 41 ] , which inserts a small trainable matrix between B B and A A to fuse more information and flexibly. Other approaches have also been explored, such as adapting low-rank values at each module [ 66 ] , incorporating the mixture-of-experts architecture [ 15 , 32 , 16 , 50 ] , exploiting multiple LoRA modules [ 59 , 28 , 30 ] , and introducing non-linear mapping [ 13 ] . In this paper, we adopt the standard two-factor modeling 2 as a first step and leave the expansion for other advanced modelings to future work.

In this paper, we proposed a Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. This metric induces new preconditioning, and we theoretically showed that this preconditioning makes LoRA better approximates full fine-tuning compared with the conventional preconditioning and no preconditioning. Diverse experiments showed the effectiveness and efficiency of our preconditioning in the language and vision domains. This paper is the first to explore the possibility of tailoring a Riemannian metric to LoRA, paving the way for future followers.

We provide the details of hyperparameters used in our experiments to ensure reproducibility. For each task, all compared methods share a common set of hyperparameters, such as the rank, batch size, weight decay, and training schedule, which are outlined in Sec. 7 . When decoding a sentence in Sec. 7.2 , we used the beam search with the beam size to 10 10 , the length penalty to 0.8 0.8 , and the no-repeat-Ngram-size to 4 4 , following [ 63 ] . For answer generation in Sec. 7.4 , we used greedy decoding with a maximum of 30 generated tokens. As mentioned in Sec. 7 , we individually tune the learning rate for each method on each validation set to ensure fair comparison. Table 6 lists the tuned learning rates for the natural language generation task in Sec. 7.2 . In this task, we tuned the learning rate over { 0.02 , 0.04 , … , 0.30 } \{0.02,0.04,\dots,0.30\} for SGD and { 0.0002 , 0.0004 , … , 0.0030 } \{0.0002,0.0004,\dots,0.0030\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. Tables 7 and 8 list the tuned learning rates for the image classification task in Sec. 7.3 and the commonsense reasoning task in Sec. 7.4 , respectively. In these tasks, we tuned the learning rate over { 0.0001 , 0.0002 , … , 0.001 } \{0.0001,0.0002,\dots,0.001\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. Note that, in the natural language generation task of Sec. 7.2 , we selected the learning rate that achieves the highest average rank (and the lowest rank variance in case of ties in the highest average rank) across the five evaluation metrics (BLEU [ 40 ] , NIST [ 12 ] , METEOR [ 3 ] , ROUGE-L [ 27 ] , and CIDEr [ 53 ] ) on the validation set. In the commonsense reasoning task of Sec. 7.4 , we selected the learning rate that achieves the top-1 validation accuracy on the validation set which is obtained by splitting Commonsense170K.

To validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning 5 for LoRA, we conducted LoRA fine-tuning experiments on natural language generation, image classification, and commonsense reasoning tasks, following the existing LoRA studies [ 21 , 63 , 56 , 41 , 26 ] . All experiments were performed in PyTorch [ 42 ] on a single H100 GPU with 80 GB VRAM. We downloaded the pre-trained models using Hugging Face Transformers library [ 57 ] .

Following [ 21 , 63 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the GPT-2 medium model [ 45 ] on E2E natural language generation challenge task [ 38 ] , which assesses the fine-tuned model’s ability to generate fluent and semantically accurate sentences from meaning representations. We followed the same experimental setup as in [ 63 ] , except that we tuned the learning rate over { 0.02 , 0.04 , … , 0.30 } \{0.02,0.04,\dots,0.30\} for SGD and { 0.0002 , 0.0004 , … , 0.0030 } \{0.0002,0.0004,\dots,0.0030\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query and value matrices of the attention layers in the GPT-2 model. We also fixed the rank to r = 4 r=4 , the scaling factor of B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} to 32 32 , the batch size to 8 8 , the dropout to 0.1 0.1 , and the train epoch to 5 5 with a linear learning-rate schedule. We set the weight decay to 0.01 0.01 for the SGD and AdamW methods. We evaluated all methods by five metrics, BLEU [ 40 ] , NIST [ 12 ] , METEOR [ 3 ] , ROUGE-L [ 27 ] , and CIDEr [ 53 ] , on the test set. Bold and underlined values indicate the highest and second-highest scores, respectively. Method Cars DTD EuroSAT GTRSB RESISC45 SUN397 SVHN Ave. AdamW 71.82 70.53 98.35 97.84 94.48 72.04 96.79 85.98 w/ 4 72.14 71.28 98.19 98.32 94.49 72.64 96.83 86.27 w/ 5 (Ours) 72.03 71.86 98.52 98.54 94.70 72.57 96.92 86.45 Table 3: Top-1 test accuracy in LoRA fine-tuning for the LLaMA2-7B model on the eight commonsense reasoning datasets with different preconditioning. Method BoolQ PIQA SIQA HellaS WinoG ARC-e ARC-c OBQA Ave. AdamW 73.33 83.41 79.38 92.36 83.74 85.77 72.87 82.60 81.68 w/ 4 74.31 84.17 77.99 93.12 83.43 86.28 74.23 82.20 81.97 w/ 5 (Ours) 73.55 83.62 79.02 92.95 85.48 86.41 74.32 83.40 82.34 Table 1 shows the results. We observed that our SGD and AdamW methods outperform other SGD and AdamW methods, respectively, across almost all metrics. Especially, our AdamW method achieves the highest scores in four metrics and the second-highest in the remaining one. These results validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning for LoRA on the language generation task.

To validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically, we investigate how preconditioning affects training time. For this purpose, we compared training times of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning. The experimental setup was the same as that described in Sec. 7.3 . The difference in training times mainly stems from dataset size and the computational cost of preconditioning. Figure 1 shows the results. Each method shows the mean and standard deviation of training times over all learning rates we used for validation. We observed that, although there are some differences due to constant time factors, the results are almost the same across all methods, including the AdamW with our preconditioning 5 as it admits the efficient implementation described in Sec. 5.1 . Consequently, these results validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically and show the computational efficiency of our preconditioning 5 . Figure 1: Training time comparison of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning.

passages.text: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. Code is available in the Molt library . \abscontent

Figure 1: Lower training memory across model scales. Colors denote model sizes; hatching distinguishes Dense Adam from LoGRA. Dark bars show average memory and pale extensions reach peak memory (Table 1 ); labels report average / peak in GiB per training GPU. Arrows show average-memory savings over Dense Adam. The broken axis omits 34–48 GiB. The 27B Dense Adam bar marks OOM at GPU capacity, not a measured value. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key driver of advances in LLM, enabling models to improve through feedback on their own generated responses ( Sheng et al., 2024 ; , 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . However, its substantial memory requirements remain a major barrier to broader adoption. This challenge extends well beyond storing model parameters, as gradients and optimizer states can consume several times more memory than the weights themselves. For example, the BF16 weights of a 7B-parameter Qwen model ( Bai et al., 2023 ) require approximately 14 GB, while Adam’s ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) two FP32 moment buffers add another 56 GB, even before accounting for gradients and activations. Consequently, hardware capable of running a model may still be insufficient to improve it through RL. Reducing this memory overhead is therefore critical to making RL post-training accessible to the broader research community.

To overcome this bottleneck, existing approaches span both system-level optimizations and memory-efficient training algorithms. At the system level, FSDP ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) shards training states across GPUs, gradient checkpointing ( Chen et al., 2016 ) reduces activation storage through recomputation, and CPU offloading moves selected training states to host memory ( Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . Parameter-efficient methods reduce the number of parameters that require gradients and optimizer states: LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) , for example, freezes pretrained weights and learns small low-rank adapters. Gradient compression offers another route ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2025 ; Hao et al., 2024 ) : they keep the original weight matrices trainable while using compact representations of gradients and optimizer states, thereby reducing training memory while still enabling effective updates to the full model.

We evaluate LoGRA across multiple reasoning tasks with models ranging from 1.5B to 27B parameters. LoGRA reduces average training memory by 21.8% at 1.5B and 45.7% at 7B without sacrificing task performance. These savings also make larger-scale training feasible: LoGRA sustains stable learning of a 27B model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where the dense Adam baseline runs out of memory under the same hardware allocation. Ablations further clarify how projection design and KL budgets affect learning performance and training stability.

Figure 3 shows that LoGRA lowers average per-update memory at 1.5B and 7B. Over the complete runs, average memory decreases from 9.18 to 7.18 GiB at 1.5B and from 31.82 to 17.29 GiB at 7B, reductions of 21.8% and 45.7%, respectively. Under the seed-averaged peak definition, LoGRA reduces peak memory from 9.19 to 8.66 GiB at 1.5B and from 31.85 to 22.26 GiB at 7B. At 27B, LoGRA uses 51.54 GiB on average and reaches a peak seed-averaged memory of 53.88 GiB; Dense fails before completing an update, precluding a measured memory-reduction ratio or throughput comparison. End-to-end update rates are similar where both methods complete training: 55.44 versus 54.28 updates/h at 1.5B and 25.73 versus 25.28 updates/h at 7B for LoGRA and Dense, respectively. The main systems benefit is reduced memory use and feasibility at 27B, with modest observed throughput gains at 1.5B and 7B.

We presented LoGRA, a memory-efficient approach to LLM RL post-training that uses low-rank gradient sketches throughout gradient accumulation, weight updates, and policy synchronization. Our results show that compact gradient representations can substantially reduce training memory without sacrificing reasoning performance. In particular, LoGRA enables sustained training of a 27B model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam exceeds the available memory. Predicted-KL step control complements compression by regulating policy changes, with conservative budgets supporting stable long-horizon learning. Together, these findings highlight gradient representation as a practical lever for lowering the hardware barrier to RL post-training.

passages.text: Tool-using agents repeatedly carry observations whose useful content can be much smaller than their original payload. We study agent-controlled forgetting: the acting model selects previously observed tool results, replaces each with a short note at its original position, and retains the exact original in a recoverable archive. A Python harness exposes batch archival and explicit recovery without task-specific model training, while protecting user instructions and assistant messages from these operations. In an exploratory OpenTelemetry debugging case followed by an unrelated implementation task, the method ended with 231,951 provider-reported prompt tokens versus 912,492 under retained history, used 50% fewer cumulative input tokens, and had an estimated API cost of $1.28–$1.44 versus approximately $4.38. Both arms passed the two-case primary behavioral oracle; neither fully satisfied the follow-up evaluation. The method made more requests and took 17% longer. A contrasting application-development pair produced no context or cost saving, and an earlier continuation exhibited lower manually assessed quality despite reduced context. These observations demonstrate substantial resource savings in noisy tool-use trajectories and identify workload dependence as a central consideration for reversible context management.

Both arms submit both tasks normally, without recorded provider errors. Table 1 shows substantial reduction in active and cumulative input under the method despite more requests. At primary submission the method carries 124,746 prompt tokens versus 847,674 for retained, an 85% reduction. After the follow-up, the method carries 231,951 versus 912,492 prompt tokens, a 75% reduction. The method peak is 381,299 versus 912,492 tokens. Thus, the observed comparison reaches a substantially larger retained context than the earlier coding tasks. Table 1. OpenTelemetry, both phases unless specified. The estimated cost is approximately 67–71% lower, even after reported cache usage is included. The method generates more than twice as many completion tokens and takes 17% longer. These are resource savings without a speed advantage in this case. Original ledgers and exact deltas are linked in the OpenTelemetry metrics.

The largest retained-context jump follows a 2,478,818-character browser_find result at primary step 74, three requests before primary submission; the follow-up then carries the accumulated history through 44 further requests. Because the arms encounter different observations and most primary implementation precedes this jump, the pair measures complete retention trajectories rather than controlled exposure to identical noise.

Selection after diagnosis. Large tool outputs can be necessary for discovering an explanation but redundant after that explanation is established. The OpenTelemetry archive illustrates that the agent can act on this distinction. Repeated input savings arise only after the initial exposure. If subsequent work is short, or if most observations remain relevant, the overhead of extra prompts, notes, and tool calls can outweigh the reduction. Planroom provides a concrete boundary case. Working with verbose external tools. The retention operation acts on recorded observations, so an upstream tool need not expose its own compaction controls. In principle, the same contract can cover documentation, diagnostic logs, browser text, and images. Its value depends on whether the agent can retain the useful evidence after inspection, not merely on the size of a response. Filtering and curation can be combined: one limits initial exposure, while the other revisits retention as the task evolves. Task pivots. A new user request supplies information about what should remain active. For example, after a diagnosis is complete, the agent can retain the finding and its source references while archiving the long observations used to establish it. Batch selection permits a separate note for each result, preserving the surrounding conversation and access to the originals rather than replacing the entire session with a single summary. The same-session continuation exercises the mechanism beyond one isolated answer. It shows that the method can continue implementing after context edits while retained history continues to grow. An identical-history branching comparison is the next step for isolating the effect of curation at the pivot itself.

Why retained history first, and context editing next. Retained history answers the initial deployment question: what changes when an acting agent gains explicit control over which tool results remain active? It measures the combined interface and prompting policy against keeping all observations. The next direct comparison should test this policy against threshold-triggered removal of older tool results, as documented in Anthropic’s context-editing documentation ( [ ref-anthropic_context_editing ] ). That comparison would ask whether task-aware selection, per-result notes, and recovery improve the resource–quality trade-off beyond automatic clearing. A controlled test should use the same acting model, tools, tasks, and output budget across conditions; a harness implementation of an analogous clearing policy must be distinguished from a test of the provider’s actual feature. This baseline is a priority for the next study and has not been evaluated in the present experiments. Cache and control. The cost result is compatible with reduced input outweighing cache disruption, but it does not identify the provider’s cache mechanics. More model decisions can coexist with lower total cost, as in OpenTelemetry, or with a small cost increase, as in Planroom. Curation frequency is consequently not a useful success metric on its own. ACON includes acting-agent and compressor calls in its practical API cost estimate but explicitly excludes input caching ( [ ref-kang_2025_acon ] ). Our accounting includes reported cache usage; the different workloads and models preclude a direct numerical comparison.

Agent-controlled forgetting provides an explicit way for a tool-using model to distinguish information it needed to inspect from information it still needs to carry. In the central noisy debugging case, reversible curation accompanies a 75% smaller final measured prompt, 50% less cumulative input, and substantially lower estimated API cost, while both arms pass the same two primary behavioral cases. The method also requires more actions and time, and follow-up correctness remains incomplete. Contrasting application development and an adverse continuation show that neither resource savings nor quality preservation follows automatically from a smaller active history. The practical result is that an agent can complete noisy tool-driven work with substantially less active context and repeated input, using explicit archival decisions during the task. The contrasting outcomes define where further comparisons and replication are needed.

Selection after diagnosis. Large tool outputs can be necessary for discovering an explanation but redundant after that explanation is established. The OpenTelemetry archive illustrates that the agent can act on this distinction. Repeated input savings arise only after the initial exposure. If subsequent work is short, or if most observations remain relevant, the overhead of extra prompts, notes, and tool calls can outweigh the reduction. Planroom provides a concrete boundary case. Working with verbose external tools. The retention operation acts on recorded observations, so an upstream tool need not expose its own compaction controls. In principle, the same contract can cover documentation, diagnostic logs, browser text, and images. Its value depends on whether the agent can retain the useful evidence after inspection, not merely on the size of a response. Filtering and curation can be combined: one limits initial exposure, while the other revisits retention as the task evolves. Task pivots. A new user request supplies information about what should remain active. For example, after a diagnosis is complete, the agent can retain the finding and its source references while archiving the long observations used to establish it. Batch selection permits a separate note for each result, preserving the surrounding conversation and access to the originals rather than replacing the entire session with a single summary. The same-session continuation exercises the mechanism beyond one isolated answer. It shows that the method can continue implementing after context edits while retained history continues to grow. An identical-history branching comparison is the next step for isolating the effect of curation at the pivot itself.

Why retained history first, and context editing next. Retained history answers the initial deployment question: what changes when an acting agent gains explicit control over which tool results remain active? It measures the combined interface and prompting policy against keeping all observations. The next direct comparison should test this policy against threshold-triggered removal of older tool results, as documented in Anthropic’s context-editing documentation ( [ ref-anthropic_context_editing ] ). That comparison would ask whether task-aware selection, per-result notes, and recovery improve the resource–quality trade-off beyond automatic clearing. A controlled test should use the same acting model, tools, tasks, and output budget across conditions; a harness implementation of an analogous clearing policy must be distinguished from a test of the provider’s actual feature. This baseline is a priority for the next study and has not been evaluated in the present experiments. Cache and control. The cost result is compatible with reduced input outweighing cache disruption, but it does not identify the provider’s cache mechanics. More model decisions can coexist with lower total cost, as in OpenTelemetry, or with a small cost increase, as in Planroom. Curation frequency is consequently not a useful success metric on its own. ACON includes acting-agent and compressor calls in its practical API cost estimate but explicitly excludes input caching ( [ ref-kang_2025_acon ] ). Our accounting includes reported cache usage; the different workloads and models preclude a direct numerical comparison.

Agent-controlled forgetting provides an explicit way for a tool-using model to distinguish information it needed to inspect from information it still needs to carry. In the central noisy debugging case, reversible curation accompanies a 75% smaller final measured prompt, 50% less cumulative input, and substantially lower estimated API cost, while both arms pass the same two primary behavioral cases. The method also requires more actions and time, and follow-up correctness remains incomplete. Contrasting application development and an adverse continuation show that neither resource savings nor quality preservation follows automatically from a smaller active history. The practical result is that an agent can complete noisy tool-driven work with substantially less active context and repeated input, using explicit archival decisions during the task. The contrasting outcomes define where further comparisons and replication are needed.

inspect:2610.06542.question: In language-model fine-tuning experiments, does the LoRA-RIP metric predict which adapter ranks work best? Which fixed-rank and data-selection baselines are compared, and what task-performance differences are measured at matched trainable-parameter and training budgets?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. Our central insight is that the appropriate adapter rank should depend on the quality of the data-induced optimization geometry, rather than on the model alone. To formalize this connection, we introduce LoRA-RIP, a data-dependent restricted-isometry metric that characterizes the conditioning of the cross-entropy (CE) objective along LoRA-relevant low-rank directions. We prove that sufficient rank over-parameterization, with the required rank explicitly determined by the LoRA-RIP constant, eliminates spurious local minima, thereby extending existing RIP-based guarantees beyond the classical 1 / 3 1/3 regime. This characterization further enables principled data selection under a fixed rank budget. Experiments across language and vision tasks support these theoretical predictions, showing that rank and data quality are two coupled resources that should be jointly considered for more efficient and reliable LoRA fine-tuning.

of landscape theory, but their reliance on local linearization or squared-loss settings limits the guidance they provide for nonlinear cross-entropy fine-tuning. More recently, Kim et al. (2025) move beyond linearization by adapting established low-rank optimization arguments ( Zhu et al., 2018 ; Ha et al., 2020 ) , showing how RIP-type conditions still govern the landscapes in nonlinear LoRA settings and providing numerical evidence for their applicability. Their global-optimality guarantee in the analyzed region corresponds to a RIP constant below 1 / 3 1/3 , while larger values allow a “fails-loudly” alternative. However, their analysis leaves two important aspects insufficiently characterized: the CE-specific structure of the RIP constant in LoRA, and how the adapter rank r r shapes the optimization landscape beyond the small-RIP regime. Since RIP is strongly determined by the geometry of the fine-tuning data, these two questions are closely connected: understanding LoRA optimization requires relating data-induced RIP to the role of rank in shaping the landscape. Clarifying this relationship is therefore a key step toward a more principled theory of rank choice in LoRA fine-tuning.

In this work, we build on theoretical tools from classical low-rank optimization and matrix sensing ( Zhang et al., 2021 ; Zhang, 2025b ; Yalçın et al., 2023 ) and extend them to develop a fine-grained landscape characterization of LoRA under cross-entropy loss. We introduce a new data-dependent LoRA-RIP constant, denoted by δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} . Under the stated assumptions, we establish an explicit relation between r / r ⋆ r/r_{\star} and δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} that guarantees a landscape free of spurious local minima, where r ⋆ r_{\star} refers to the rank of the global solution. This implies that any algorithm that can converge to a second-order stationary point (SOSP) 1 1 1 For definition of SOSP please see Appendix B.1 in polynomial time can reach the global solution reliably. More importantly, our results hold in the regime where δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} exceeds 1 / 3 1/3 , and show that larger ranks permit larger LoRA-RIP values in the guarantee. Under common curvature bounds covering the ranks considered, this characterization yields a sufficient constant-factor rank requirement relative to r ⋆ r_{\star} , with the factor determined by the LoRA-RIP bound. Once this requirement is met, further rank is unnecessary for the same guarantee within that range. Therefore it means that in most LoRA settings, r r does not need to be excessively large to ensure good performance, preserving its parameter efficiency. Viewed from the data side, the same relationship suggests a complementary route to effective fine-tuning: improving the optimization geometry through data selection under a fixed rank budget. We therefore analyze the CE-specific structure of LoRA-RIP, revealing how certain properties of fine-tuning data affect its value

ptimization geometry through data selection under a fixed rank budget. We therefore analyze the CE-specific structure of LoRA-RIP, revealing how certain properties of fine-tuning data affect its value and deriving corresponding data-selection principles. Together, these results connect rank requirements with data composition, providing theoretical guidance for choosing adapter rank and selecting data for more parameter-and data-efficient LoRA fine-tuning.

We studied how adapter rank and fine-tuning data jointly shape LoRA’s optimization landscape under cross-entropy loss. Under the stated assumptions, rank over-parameterization relative to the target rank rules out spurious local minima, with the required factor explicitly determined by our data-dependent LoRA-RIP constant δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} . The guarantee also covers LoRA-RIP values above 1 / 3 1/3 , quantifying how additional rank can compensate for less favorable geometry to achieve a benign landscape. Our framework further motivates data selection under a fixed rank budget, yielding principles based on latent-space coverage and pre-tuning softmax saturation. Experiments support these insights into the interplay between rank and data composition. However, most of the bounds presented in this work are sufficient, and an important future direction is to shorten their gap with necessary ones.

Our theoretical analysis focuses on single-matrix LoRA fine-tuning with cross-entropy loss under low-rank target and LoRA-RIP assumptions. The resulting rank bounds are sufficient rather than necessary, leaving room for tighter characterizations of the relationship between adapter rank and data-induced geometry. Our empirical evaluation examines this relationship through controlled classification experiments across datasets and backbones. Extending the theory to joint multi-layer adaptation and evaluating the data-selection principles in larger-scale generative fine-tuning are natural directions for future work.

inspect:2610.06621.question: For Frozen Factor or Spectral Band, which language-model tasks and baselines test frozen A versus frozen B and top versus bottom singular directions? Were rank, trainable-parameter count, learning-rate tuning, and training budget controlled, and what performance differences and limitations were measured?

passages.text: Spectral variants of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) choose both a subspace and which factor to freeze. We separate these choices by freezing the input factor A A or output factor B B on the top or bottom singular directions of pretrained weights, with learning rates selected separately. At rank 2, the same-band advantage of freezing A A is larger than either within-factor band difference on all four task–model pairs with complete comparisons. Freezing B B also trails comparable-budget free LoRA by 8–18 percentage points on five pairs spanning a formatting task and OpenBookQA. The A-frozen advantage persists in a single-GPU-model replication and within individual MLP module groups, including controls with equal or greater trainable counts for B frozen, and when A is frozen on a random orthonormal basis. The factor contrast weakens with rank. On OpenBookQA / Qwen2.5-1.5B at rank 16, PEFT’s MiCA implementation trails comparable-budget LoRA by 3.08 points under a shared training recipe transferred from the MiCA paper. A trained oracle output subspace largely removes the low-rank deficit; partial warm-up gains recur across three direction seeds. The factor-versus-band ordering is descriptive; an approximate multiplicity audit weakens several earlier significance claims. These results extend known factor asymmetry by showing how its magnitude depends on spectral placement, rank and training conditions.

LoRA adapts a pretrained weight matrix through a low-rank update B ​ A BA , where A A maps the layer input into a small intermediate representation and B B maps that representation to the output ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Fixing one factor reduces the number of trainable parameters, but also fixes either the input or output subspace available to the update. A spectral construction makes another choice: which singular directions of the pretrained weight should define that subspace? Cross-method comparisons can entangle these choices. MiCA fixes the output factor on bottom singular directions ( Rüdiger and Raschka, 2026 ) ; PiCa’s implementation fixes an input-side projector on top directions and shares the trainable output factor across layers ( Hwang et al., 2026 ) . These correspond to freezing B B and A A , respectively (Appendix C.3 ). Comparing them changes orientation, band and sharing at once. Their within-method band ablations, by contrast, hold orientation fixed. The asymmetry between LoRA factors is already known. Zhu et al. (2024) show that training B B while fixing A A is often more effective than the reverse, including experiments with spectral factors. LoRA-FA fixes A A for memory efficiency ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and LoRA+ improves training by assigning a larger learning rate to B B ( Hayou et al., 2024a ) . The question we address is narrower: how large is the frozen-factor contrast relative to the top-versus-bottom spectral contrast, and how does that comparison change with rank?

We use a two-by-two design: freeze A A or B B , each on the top or bottom band, while retaining the same pretrained model, data, adapted modules and training budget. Learning rates are selected separately for every configuration. We complement equal-rank comparisons with free LoRA at a nearby trainable-parameter count and a control that gives the B-frozen configuration more parameters than the A-frozen configuration. Figure 1 illustrates the main low-rank result. Figure 1: At rank 2, changing the frozen factor has a larger effect than switching spectral extremes. Points are mean test scores over five seeds at separately selected learning rates. The free-LoRA reference has rank 1 and a comparable, slightly larger trainable budget than rank-2 B-frozen LoRA. A-frozen LoRA has more trainable parameters at equal rank; Table 3 controls this advantage. The panels use different vertical scales. Lines connect configurations, not training trajectories. Full scores and uncertainty are in Tables 7 and 2 . At rank 2, the factor contrast exceeds the band contrast on all four complete comparisons. The A-frozen advantage survives parameter-count and module-group controls and does not require a spectral input basis on the two pairs tested. The factor contrast decreases along the complete OpenBookQA rank sweep, becoming comparable to the band contrast at rank 16. Finally, a subspace extracted from trained LoRA greatly improves B-frozen performance, showing that its low-rank deficit depends on placement.

Our contribution is to separate these design choices under optimization and budget controls and identify the limits of the resulting comparison. Factor asymmetry itself is not new. A follow-up evaluates PEFT’s MiCA implementation under a transferred recipe, without reproducing its original knowledge-acquisition benchmark or evaluating PiCa.

passages.section: 3.3 Training controls and remaining optimization effects
passages.text: Three controls test narrower alternatives. On Llama’s formatting task, quadrupling the supervised-token budget and retuning every learning rate reduces the cost of fixing B B , but leaves equal-rank deficits of 12.0 and 18.2 points relative to training both factors. A fresh five-seed replication also retains the large gap; its factor contrast is 15.21 points versus an absolute band contrast of 2.96 points. On OpenBookQA with Qwen2.5-1.5B, supervising answers only preserves A-frozen advantages of 7.2 and 9.7 points. This last control holds the number of optimizer steps and the packed sequences fixed, while reducing supervised tokens by about sixfold; it tests loss masking rather than an equal-supervision training regime. Appendix E gives the measurements. Making both factors trainable from the same spectral initialization also restores most of the performance, including at the comparable-budget rank. Once B B is trainable, however, it can leave the initial band. The disappearance of a band difference in this control is therefore expected and is not independent evidence that the original band was irrelevant. The data also leave room for optimization effects. On the formatting task, fixed singular-value scaling improves the top-band B-frozen score by 3.61 points, and a fixed scalar per module improves it by 2.31 points without changing the accessible subspace. The scalar is determined from the pretrained spectrum; it is not an extra learned parameter. Loss curves continue to decrease at the original training endpoint. These observations prevent interpreting the remaining gap as a measured approximation-error floor.

passages.section: 3.3 Training controls and remaining optimization effects
passages.text: A separate replication reruns all seven central formatting configurations on RTX 4000 Ada at their original selected rates. The A-frozen advantages are 13.16 and 19.67 points (top and bottom), and the free-LoRA gaps are 12.74 and 18.66 points. All retain their campaign decisions. This removes differences in GPU model as an explanation for this replication, while leaving the historical scores unchanged (Appendix E.1 ).

inspect:2610.14393.question: What are SciCurateBench’s paper-classification and retrieval baselines, evaluation controls, and measured gains on LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC? Which parts of LangPoli apply to general research-paper retrieval rather than life-science-specific data curation?

passages.text: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scicuratebench-D885/ .

We show that popular LLM reasoning methods achieve only suboptimal performance on the benchmark. To further push performance and study the factors contributing to success, we propose LangPoli, a multi-agent framework that adaptively creates tools to retrieve information from heterogeneous documents and verify precise conditions in the query. Unlike code-action agents that couple planning and implementation in a single generation step, LangPoli separates a natural-language policy from environment-specific code synthesis. matches.title: Lightweight and Versatile Learned Optimization by Recombination of Gradient History
matches.abstract_excerpt: This paper presents a lightweight and versatile learned optimizer that dynamically recombines gradient history, represented as averages over disjoint time spans. passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. 2610.10965:c384434acebe73b9b8bb5ab2558b7.question: In the NanoGPT speedruns, how does Spectrally Targeted Muon compare with full Muon and other optimizer baselines on validation loss and training cost? Which singular-value directions are targeted, and how do the measured weight effective ranks change?

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

The Muon optimizer for deep learning works by orthogonalizing the update matrix ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) . Unlike many other proposed optimizers, this has been highly successful empirically for training large language models, especially when coupled with weight decay ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . This is because the matrix can be orthogonalized relatively efficiently, using methods such as Newton-Schulz or Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . The orthogonalization step can be thought of as applying the matrix sign function to the gradient matrix, which normalizes all the singular values to one, prompting the question of whether Muon’s success comes from amplifying small but important directions with small singular values ignored by standard gradient descent, or from normalizing large, degenerate directions with large singular values that misdirect the training. In this paper, we will explore a method to target this orthogonalization to singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ \tau , and we will also experiment with different values for this threshold, thus allowing us to interpolate between SGD and Muon with a spectrally targeted version. Specifically, we will apply these Muon variants to the two speedrun tasks originally used to show Muon’s performance, the CIFAR-10 dataset with a convolutional network, and the NanoGPT large language model, just as in Jordan et al. (2024b) . In addition to standard performance metrics, we will examine other metrics more pertinent to the linear-algebraic structure of our weight and update matrices. This allows us to explore what characteristics of matrix optimizers lead to richer learning.

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

The Muon optimizer for deep learning works by orthogonalizing the update matrix ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) . Unlike many other proposed optimizers, this has been highly successful empirically for training large language models, especially when coupled with weight decay ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . This is because the matrix can be orthogonalized relatively efficiently, using methods such as Newton-Schulz or Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . The orthogonalization step can be thought of as applying the matrix sign function to the gradient matrix, which normalizes all the singular values to one, prompting the question of whether Muon’s success comes from amplifying small but important directions with small singular values ignored by standard gradient descent, or from normalizing large, degenerate directions with large singular values that misdirect the training. In this paper, we will explore a method to target this orthogonalization to singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ \tau , and we will also experiment with different values for this threshold, thus allowing us to interpolate between SGD and Muon with a spectrally targeted version. Specifically, we will apply these Muon variants to the two speedrun tasks originally used to show Muon’s performance, the CIFAR-10 dataset with a convolutional network, and the NanoGPT large language model, just as in Jordan et al. (2024b) . In addition to standard performance metrics, we will examine other metrics more pertinent to the linear-algebraic structure of our weight and update matrices. This allows us to explore what characteristics of matrix optimizers lead to richer learning.
