passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The advantage of ORCA holds over a wide range of learning rates: at every learning rate evaluated for both methods, ORCA reaches a lower final validation loss than Muon, and at all evaluated configurations between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} it is even better than fully tuned Muon. The independent searches select 1.3 × 10 − 3 1.3\times 10^{-3} , 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} for Adam, Muon, Pion, and ORCA, with final validation losses of 2.8824 2.8824 , 2.8460 2.8460 , 2.9790 2.9790 , and 2.8106 2.8106 , respectively; ORCA thus lowers the loss by a further 0.0354 0.0354 relative to the best Muon and stays within 0.002 0.002 of its own optimum across 1.6 × 10 − 3 1.6\times 10^{-3} to 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , showing that the improvement does not rely on a narrow learning-rate choice. LLama Pretraining Tasks. We compare ORCA against Adam and Muon on LLaMA 350M and 1.3B, training each model for 100B tokens. As shown in Figure 4.1 , Muon outperforms Adam at both scales, while ORCA further lowers the validation loss. Compared with Muon, ORCA reduces the final loss by 0.0194 0.0194 at 350M and 0.0244 0.0244 at 1.3B, with consistent gains at both scales. Further, a four-seed robustness result for the 130M, 50k-step setting is reported in Appendix C . We also evaluate the final ORCA and Muon LLaMA 1.3B checkpoints from Figure 4.1 on five downstream tasks ( Clark et al., 2018 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ) . As shown in Table 4.1 , ORCA outperforms Muon on all five tasks. This suggests that the lower pre-training loss of ORCA also leads to better downstream performance.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. We use top- 4 4 routing with 64 64 experts in the MoE 0.8 0.8 B model ( 0.24 0.24 B active parameters) and 64 64 experts in the MoE 8 8 B model ( 1 1 B active parameters) ( Dai et al., 2024 ) . Due to computational budget constraints, we focus our comparison on Muon and ORCA. ORCA achieves the lowest final loss at both 25 25 B and 50 50 B tokens for the 0.8 0.8 B model, showing that its gain persists as the token budget increases. The 8 8 B experiment extends this result to a larger model trained on 100 100 B tokens, where ORCA also finishes below Muon ( Figure 4.4 ). passages.text: Recent progress of foundation models with deep neural networks, such as large vision and large language models, has been remarkable [ 39 , 17 , 10 , 61 , 2 ] . When transferring these pre-trained models to a specific downstream task, one popular technique is full fine-tuning that updates all the model parameters. However, full fine-tuning of large foundation models is impractical due to their large number of parameters, requiring high computational and storage costs for each task-specific model. To address this issue, parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques have become a promising alternative to full fine-tuning [ 25 , 44 , 21 , 22 , 18 ] . Among these techniques, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto standard thanks to its simplicity and effectiveness [ 21 ] . Let W 0 , W ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0},W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} denote the weight matrices of a layer in the pre-trained and fine-tuned models, respectively. passages.text: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. Code is available in the Molt library . \abscontent

Figure 1: Lower training memory across model scales. Colors denote model sizes; hatching distinguishes Dense Adam from LoGRA. Dark bars show average memory and pale extensions reach peak memory (Table 1 ); labels report average / peak in GiB per training GPU. Arrows show average-memory savings over Dense Adam. The broken axis omits 34–48 GiB. The 27B Dense Adam bar marks OOM at GPU capacity, not a measured value. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key driver of advances in LLM, enabling models to improve through feedback on their own generated responses ( Sheng et al., 2024 ; , 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . However, its substantial memory requirements remain a major barrier to broader adoption. This challenge extends well beyond storing model parameters, as gradients and optimizer states can consume several times more memory than the weights themselves. For example, the BF16 weights of a 7B-parameter Qwen model ( Bai et al., 2023 ) require approximately 14 GB, while Adam’s ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) two FP32 moment buffers add another 56 GB, even before accounting for gradients and activations. Consequently, hardware capable of running a model may still be insufficient to improve it through RL. Reducing this memory overhead is therefore critical to making RL post-training accessible to the broader research community.

To overcome this bottleneck, existing approaches span both system-level optimizations and memory-efficient training algorithms. At the system level, FSDP ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) shards training states across GPUs, gradient checkpointing ( Chen et al., 2016 ) reduces activation storage through recomputation, and CPU offloading moves selected training states to host memory ( Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . Parameter-efficient methods reduce the number of parameters that require gradients and optimizer states: LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) , for example, freezes pretrained weights and learns small low-rank adapters. Gradient compression offers another route ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2025 ; Hao et al., 2024 ) : they keep the original weight matrices trainable while using compact representations of gradients and optimizer states, thereby reducing training memory while still enabling effective updates to the full model.

We evaluate LoGRA across multiple reasoning tasks with models ranging from 1.5B to 27B parameters. LoGRA reduces average training memory by 21.8% at 1.5B and 45.7% at 7B without sacrificing task performance. These savings also make larger-scale training feasible: LoGRA sustains stable learning of a 27B model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where the dense Adam baseline runs out of memory under the same hardware allocation. Ablations further clarify how projection design and KL budgets affect learning performance and training stability.

Figure 3 shows that LoGRA lowers average per-update memory at 1.5B and 7B. Over the complete runs, average memory decreases from 9.18 to 7.18 GiB at 1.5B and from 31.82 to 17.29 GiB at 7B, reductions of 21.8% and 45.7%, respectively. Under the seed-averaged peak definition, LoGRA reduces peak memory from 9.19 to 8.66 GiB at 1.5B and from 31.85 to 22.26 GiB at 7B. At 27B, LoGRA uses 51.54 GiB on average and reaches a peak seed-averaged memory of 53.88 GiB; Dense fails before completing an update, precluding a measured memory-reduction ratio or throughput comparison. End-to-end update rates are similar where both methods complete training: 55.44 versus 54.28 updates/h at 1.5B and 25.73 versus 25.28 updates/h at 7B for LoGRA and Dense, respectively. The main systems benefit is reduced memory use and feasibility at 27B, with modest observed throughput gains at 1.5B and 7B.

We presented LoGRA, a memory-efficient approach to LLM RL post-training that uses low-rank gradient sketches throughout gradient accumulation, weight updates, and policy synchronization. Our results show that compact gradient representations can substantially reduce training memory without sacrificing reasoning performance. In particular, LoGRA enables sustained training of a 27B model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam exceeds the available memory. Predicted-KL step control complements compression by regulating policy changes, with conservative budgets supporting stable long-horizon learning. Together, these findings highlight gradient representation as a practical lever for lowering the hardware barrier to RL post-training.

2610.10590:ddaf222d6eed912895396f4ac3f6d.question: How were the retained-history and reversible-archival agent harnesses compared on task success, cumulative input tokens, latency, and cost? What failures or negative-control cases limit the reported savings?

passages.text: Tool-using agents repeatedly carry observations whose useful content can be much smaller than their original payload. We study agent-controlled forgetting: the acting model selects previously observed tool results, replaces each with a short note at its original position, and retains the exact original in a recoverable archive. A Python harness exposes batch archival and explicit recovery without task-specific model training, while protecting user instructions and assistant messages from these operations. In an exploratory OpenTelemetry debugging case followed by an unrelated implementation task, the method ended with 231,951 provider-reported prompt tokens versus 912,492 under retained history, used 50% fewer cumulative input tokens, and had an estimated API cost of $1.28–$1.44 versus approximately $4.38. Both arms passed the two-case primary behavioral oracle; neither fully satisfied the follow-up evaluation. The method made more requests and took 17% longer. A contrasting application-development pair produced no context or cost saving, and an earlier continuation exhibited lower manually assessed quality despite reduced context. These observations demonstrate substantial resource savings in noisy tool-use trajectories and identify workload dependence as a central consideration for reversible context management.

Both arms submit both tasks normally, without recorded provider errors. Table 1 shows substantial reduction in active and cumulative input under the method despite more requests. At primary submission the method carries 124,746 prompt tokens versus 847,674 for retained, an 85% reduction. After the follow-up, the method carries 231,951 versus 912,492 prompt tokens, a 75% reduction. The method peak is 381,299 versus 912,492 tokens. Thus, the observed comparison reaches a substantially larger retained context than the earlier coding tasks. Table 1. OpenTelemetry, both phases unless specified. The estimated cost is approximately 67–71% lower, even after reported cache usage is included. The method generates more than twice as many completion tokens and takes 17% longer. These are resource savings without a speed advantage in this case. Original ledgers and exact deltas are linked in the OpenTelemetry metrics.

The largest retained-context jump follows a 2,478,818-character browser_find result at primary step 74, three requests before primary submission; the follow-up then carries the accumulated history through 44 further requests. Because the arms encounter different observations and most primary implementation precedes this jump, the pair measures complete retention trajectories rather than controlled exposure to identical noise.

Selection after diagnosis. Large tool outputs can be necessary for discovering an explanation but redundant after that explanation is established. The OpenTelemetry archive illustrates that the agent can act on this distinction. Repeated input savings arise only after the initial exposure. If subsequent work is short, or if most observations remain relevant, the overhead of extra prompts, notes, and tool calls can outweigh the reduction. Planroom provides a concrete boundary case. Working with verbose external tools. The retention operation acts on recorded observations, so an upstream tool need not expose its own compaction controls. In principle, the same contract can cover documentation, diagnostic logs, browser text, and images. Its value depends on whether the agent can retain the useful evidence after inspection, not merely on the size of a response. Filtering and curation can be combined: one limits initial exposure, while the other revisits retention as the task evolves. Task pivots. A new user request supplies information about what should remain active. For example, after a diagnosis is complete, the agent can retain the finding and its source references while archiving the long observations used to establish it. Batch selection permits a separate note for each result, preserving the surrounding conversation and access to the originals rather than replacing the entire session with a single summary. The same-session continuation exercises the mechanism beyond one isolated answer. It shows that the method can continue implementing after context edits while retained history continues to grow. An identical-history branching comparison is the next step for isolating the effect of curation at the pivot itself.

Why retained history first, and context editing next. Retained history answers the initial deployment question: what changes when an acting agent gains explicit control over which tool results remain active? It measures the combined interface and prompting policy against keeping all observations. The next direct comparison should test this policy against threshold-triggered removal of older tool results, as documented in Anthropic’s context-editing documentation ( [ ref-anthropic_context_editing ] ). That comparison would ask whether task-aware selection, per-result notes, and recovery improve the resource–quality trade-off beyond automatic clearing. A controlled test should use the same acting model, tools, tasks, and output budget across conditions; a harness implementation of an analogous clearing policy must be distinguished from a test of the provider’s actual feature. This baseline is a priority for the next study and has not been evaluated in the present experiments. Cache and control. The cost result is compatible with reduced input outweighing cache disruption, but it does not identify the provider’s cache mechanics. More model decisions can coexist with lower total cost, as in OpenTelemetry, or with a small cost increase, as in Planroom. Curation frequency is consequently not a useful success metric on its own. ACON includes acting-agent and compressor calls in its practical API cost estimate but explicitly excludes input caching ( [ ref-kang_2025_acon ] ). Our accounting includes reported cache usage; the different workloads and models preclude a direct numerical comparison.

Agent-controlled forgetting provides an explicit way for a tool-using model to distinguish information it needed to inspect from information it still needs to carry. In the central noisy debugging case, reversible curation accompanies a 75% smaller final measured prompt, 50% less cumulative input, and substantially lower estimated API cost, while both arms pass the same two primary behavioral cases. The method also requires more actions and time, and follow-up correctness remains incomplete. Contrasting application development and an adverse continuation show that neither resource savings nor quality preservation follows automatically from a smaller active history. The practical result is that an agent can complete noisy tool-driven work with substantially less active context and repeated input, using explicit archival decisions during the task. The contrasting outcomes define where further comparisons and replication are needed.

If subsequent work is short, or if most observations remain relevant, the overhead of extra prompts, notes, and tool calls can outweigh the reduction. Planroom provides a concrete boundary case. Working with verbose external tools. The retention operation acts on recorded observations, so an upstream tool need not expose its own compaction controls. In principle, the same contract can cover documentation, diagnostic logs, browser text, and images. Its value depends on whether the agent can retain the useful evidence after inspection, not merely on the size of a response. Filtering and curation can be combined: one limits initial exposure, while the other revisits retention as the task evolves. Task pivots. A new user request supplies information about what should remain active. For example, after a diagnosis is complete, the agent can retain the finding and its source references while archiving the long observations used to establish it. Batch selection permits a separate note for each result, preserving the surrounding conversation and access to the originals rather than replacing the entire session with a single summary. The same-session continuation exercises the mechanism beyond one isolated answer. It shows that the method can continue implementing after context edits while retained history continues to grow. An identical-history branching comparison is the next step for isolating the effect of curation at the pivot itself.

Why retained history first, and context editing next. Retained history answers the initial deployment question: what changes when an acting agent gains explicit control over which tool results remain active? It measures the combined interface and prompting policy against keeping all observations. The next direct comparison should test this policy against threshold-triggered removal of older tool results, as documented in Anthropic’s context-editing documentation ( [ ref-anthropic_context_editing ] ). That comparison would ask whether task-aware selection, per-result notes, and recovery improve the resource–quality trade-off beyond automatic clearing. A controlled test should use the same acting model, tools, tasks, and output budget across conditions; a harness implementation of an analogous clearing policy must be distinguished from a test of the provider’s actual feature. This baseline is a priority for the next study and has not been evaluated in the present experiments. Cache and control. The cost result is compatible with reduced input outweighing cache disruption, but it does not identify the provider’s cache mechanics. More model decisions can coexist with lower total cost, as in OpenTelemetry, or with a small cost increase, as in Planroom. Curation frequency is consequently not a useful success metric on its own. ACON includes acting-agent and compressor calls in its practical API cost estimate but explicitly excludes input caching ( [ ref-kang_2025_acon ] ). Our accounting includes reported cache usage; the different workloads and models preclude a direct numerical comparison.

Agent-controlled forgetting provides an explicit way for a tool-using model to distinguish information it needed to inspect from information it still needs to carry. In the central noisy debugging case, reversible curation accompanies a 75% smaller final measured prompt, 50% less cumulative input, and substantially lower estimated API cost, while both arms pass the same two primary behavioral cases. The method also requires more actions and time, and follow-up correctness remains incomplete. Contrasting application development and an adverse continuation show that neither resource savings nor quality preservation follows automatically from a smaller active history. The practical result is that an agent can complete noisy tool-driven work with substantially less active context and repeated input, using explicit archival decisions during the task. The contrasting outcomes define where further comparisons and replication are needed.

2610.06542:3eef72ce27292acb757b1f1e81699.question: In language-model fine-tuning experiments, does the LoRA-RIP metric predict which adapter ranks work best? Which fixed-rank and data-selection baselines are compared, and what task-performance differences are measured at matched trainable-parameter and training budgets?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. Our central insight is that the appropriate adapter rank should depend on the quality of the data-induced optimization geometry, rather than on the model alone. To formalize this connection, we introduce LoRA-RIP, a data-dependent restricted-isometry metric that characterizes the conditioning of the cross-entropy (CE) objective along LoRA-relevant low-rank directions. We prove that sufficient rank over-parameterization, with the required rank explicitly determined by the LoRA-RIP constant, eliminates spurious local minima, thereby extending existing RIP-based guarantees beyond the classical 1 / 3 1/3 regime. This characterization further enables principled data selection under a fixed rank budget. Experiments across language and vision tasks support these theoretical predictions, showing that rank and data quality are two coupled resources that should be jointly considered for more efficient and reliable LoRA fine-tuning.

of landscape theory, but their reliance on local linearization or squared-loss settings limits the guidance they provide for nonlinear cross-entropy fine-tuning. More recently, Kim et al. (2025) move beyond linearization by adapting established low-rank optimization arguments ( Zhu et al., 2018 ; Ha et al., 2020 ) , showing how RIP-type conditions still govern the landscapes in nonlinear LoRA settings and providing numerical evidence for their applicability. Their global-optimality guarantee in the analyzed region corresponds to a RIP constant below 1 / 3 1/3 , while larger values allow a “fails-loudly” alternative. However, their analysis leaves two important aspects insufficiently characterized: the CE-specific structure of the RIP constant in LoRA, and how the adapter rank r r shapes the optimization landscape beyond the small-RIP regime. Since RIP is strongly determined by the geometry of the fine-tuning data, these two questions are closely connected: understanding LoRA optimization requires relating data-induced RIP to the role of rank in shaping the landscape. Clarifying this relationship is therefore a key step toward a more principled theory of rank choice in LoRA fine-tuning.

In this work, we build on theoretical tools from classical low-rank optimization and matrix sensing ( Zhang et al., 2021 ; Zhang, 2025b ; Yalçın et al., 2023 ) and extend them to develop a fine-grained landscape characterization of LoRA under cross-entropy loss. We introduce a new data-dependent LoRA-RIP constant, denoted by δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} . Under the stated assumptions, we establish an explicit relation between r / r ⋆ r/r_{\star} and δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} that guarantees a landscape free of spurious local minima, where r ⋆ r_{\star} refers to the rank of the global solution. This implies that any algorithm that can converge to a second-order stationary point (SOSP) 1 1 1 For definition of SOSP please see Appendix B.1 in polynomial time can reach the global solution reliably. More importantly, our results hold in the regime where δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} exceeds 1 / 3 1/3 , and show that larger ranks permit larger LoRA-RIP values in the guarantee. Under common curvature bounds covering the ranks considered, this characterization yields a sufficient constant-factor rank requirement relative to r ⋆ r_{\star} , with the factor determined by the LoRA-RIP bound. Once this requirement is met, further rank is unnecessary for the same guarantee within that range. Therefore it means that in most LoRA settings, r r does not need to be excessively large to ensure good performance, preserving its parameter efficiency. Viewed from the data side, the same relationship suggests a complementary route to effective fine-tuning: improving the optimization geometry through data selection under a fixed rank budget. We therefore analyze the CE-specific structure of LoRA-RIP, revealing how certain properties of fine-tuning data affect its value and deriving corresponding data-selection principles. Together, these results connect rank requirements with data composition, providing theoretical guidance for choosing adapter rank and selecting data for more parameter-and data-efficient LoRA fine-tuning.

We studied how adapter rank and fine-tuning data jointly shape LoRA’s optimization landscape under cross-entropy loss. Under the stated assumptions, rank over-parameterization relative to the target rank rules out spurious local minima, with the required factor explicitly determined by our data-dependent LoRA-RIP constant δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} . The guarantee also covers LoRA-RIP values above 1 / 3 1/3 , quantifying how additional rank can compensate for less favorable geometry to achieve a benign landscape. Our framework further motivates data selection under a fixed rank budget, yielding principles based on latent-space coverage and pre-tuning softmax saturation. Experiments support these insights into the interplay between rank and data composition. However, most of the bounds presented in this work are sufficient, and an important future direction is to shorten their gap with necessary ones.

Our theoretical analysis focuses on single-matrix LoRA fine-tuning with cross-entropy loss under low-rank target and LoRA-RIP assumptions. The resulting rank bounds are sufficient rather than necessary, leaving room for tighter characterizations of the relationship between adapter rank and data-induced geometry. Our empirical evaluation examines this relationship through controlled classification experiments across datasets and backbones. Extending the theory to joint multi-layer adaptation and evaluating the data-selection principles in larger-scale generative fine-tuning are natural directions for future work.

2610.06621:77f08db461d25a1cdfe6ce31ced9c.question: For Frozen Factor or Spectral Band, which language-model tasks and baselines test frozen A versus frozen B and top versus bottom singular directions? Were rank, trainable-parameter count, learning-rate tuning, and training budget controlled, and what performance differences and limitations were measured?

passages.text: Spectral variants of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) choose both a subspace and which factor to freeze. We separate these choices by freezing the input factor A A or output factor B B on the top or bottom singular directions of pretrained weights, with learning rates selected separately. At rank 2, the same-band advantage of freezing A A is larger than either within-factor band difference on all four task–model pairs with complete comparisons. Freezing B B also trails comparable-budget free LoRA by 8–18 percentage points on five pairs spanning a formatting task and OpenBookQA. The A-frozen advantage persists in a single-GPU-model replication and within individual MLP module groups, including controls with equal or greater trainable counts for B frozen, and when A is frozen on a random orthonormal basis. The factor contrast weakens with rank. On OpenBookQA / Qwen2.5-1.5B at rank 16, PEFT’s MiCA implementation trails comparable-budget LoRA by 3.08 points under a shared training recipe transferred from the MiCA paper. A trained oracle output subspace largely removes the low-rank deficit; partial warm-up gains recur across three direction seeds. The factor-versus-band ordering is descriptive; an approximate multiplicity audit weakens several earlier significance claims. These results extend known factor asymmetry by showing how its magnitude depends on spectral placement, rank and training conditions.

LoRA adapts a pretrained weight matrix through a low-rank update B ​ A BA , where A A maps the layer input into a small intermediate representation and B B maps that representation to the output ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Fixing one factor reduces the number of trainable parameters, but also fixes either the input or output subspace available to the update. A spectral construction makes another choice: which singular directions of the pretrained weight should define that subspace? Cross-method comparisons can entangle these choices. MiCA fixes the output factor on bottom singular directions ( Rüdiger and Raschka, 2026 ) ; PiCa’s implementation fixes an input-side projector on top directions and shares the trainable output factor across layers ( Hwang et al., 2026 ) . These correspond to freezing B B and A A , respectively (Appendix C.3 ). Comparing them changes orientation, band and sharing at once. Their within-method band ablations, by contrast, hold orientation fixed. The asymmetry between LoRA factors is already known. Zhu et al. (2024) show that training B B while fixing A A is often more effective than the reverse, including experiments with spectral factors. LoRA-FA fixes A A for memory efficiency ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and LoRA+ improves training by assigning a larger learning rate to B B ( Hayou et al., 2024a ) . The question we address is narrower: how large is the frozen-factor contrast relative to the top-versus-bottom spectral contrast, and how does that comparison change with rank?

We use a two-by-two design: freeze A A or B B , each on the top or bottom band, while retaining the same pretrained model, data, adapted modules and training budget. Learning rates are selected separately for every configuration. We complement equal-rank comparisons with free LoRA at a nearby trainable-parameter count and a control that gives the B-frozen configuration more parameters than the A-frozen configuration. Figure 1 illustrates the main low-rank result. Figure 1: At rank 2, changing the frozen factor has a larger effect than switching spectral extremes. Points are mean test scores over five seeds at separately selected learning rates. The free-LoRA reference has rank 1 and a comparable, slightly larger trainable budget than rank-2 B-frozen LoRA. A-frozen LoRA has more trainable parameters at equal rank; Table 3 controls this advantage. The panels use different vertical scales. Lines connect configurations, not training trajectories. Full scores and uncertainty are in Tables 7 and 2 . At rank 2, the factor contrast exceeds the band contrast on all four complete comparisons. The A-frozen advantage survives parameter-count and module-group controls and does not require a spectral input basis on the two pairs tested. The factor contrast decreases along the complete OpenBookQA rank sweep, becoming comparable to the band contrast at rank 16. Finally, a subspace extracted from trained LoRA greatly improves B-frozen performance, showing that its low-rank deficit depends on placement.

Our contribution is to separate these design choices under optimization and budget controls and identify the limits of the resulting comparison. Factor asymmetry itself is not new. A follow-up evaluates PEFT’s MiCA implementation under a transferred recipe, without reproducing its original knowledge-acquisition benchmark or evaluating PiCa.

passages.section: 3.3 Training controls and remaining optimization effects
passages.text: Three controls test narrower alternatives. On Llama’s formatting task, quadrupling the supervised-token budget and retuning every learning rate reduces the cost of fixing B B , but leaves equal-rank deficits of 12.0 and 18.2 points relative to training both factors. A fresh five-seed replication also retains the large gap; its factor contrast is 15.21 points versus an absolute band contrast of 2.96 points. On OpenBookQA with Qwen2.5-1.5B, supervising answers only preserves A-frozen advantages of 7.2 and 9.7 points. This last control holds the number of optimizer steps and the packed sequences fixed, while reducing supervised tokens by about sixfold; it tests loss masking rather than an equal-supervision training regime. Appendix E gives the measurements. Making both factors trainable from the same spectral initialization also restores most of the performance, including at the comparable-budget rank. Once B B is trainable, however, it can leave the initial band. The disappearance of a band difference in this control is therefore expected and is not independent evidence that the original band was irrelevant. The data also leave room for optimization effects. On the formatting task, fixed singular-value scaling improves the top-band B-frozen score by 3.61 points, and a fixed scalar per module improves it by 2.31 points without changing the accessible subspace. The scalar is determined from the pretrained spectrum; it is not an extra learned parameter. Loss curves continue to decrease at the original training endpoint. These observations prevent interpreting the remaining gap as a measured approximation-error floor.

passages.section: 3.3 Training controls and remaining optimization effects
passages.text: A separate replication reruns all seven central formatting configurations on RTX 4000 Ada at their original selected rates. The A-frozen advantages are 13.16 and 19.67 points (top and bottom), and the free-LoRA gaps are 12.74 and 18.66 points. All retain their campaign decisions. This removes differences in GPU model as an explanation for this replication, while leaving the historical scores unchanged (Appendix E.1 ).

2610.14393:efd1df8503e34176a89c21206e0ff.question: What are SciCurateBench’s paper-classification and retrieval baselines, evaluation controls, and measured gains on LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC? Which parts of LangPoli apply to general research-paper retrieval rather than life-science-specific data curation?

passages.text: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scicuratebench-D885/ .

We show that popular LLM reasoning methods achieve only suboptimal performance on the benchmark. To further push performance and study the factors contributing to success, we propose LangPoli, a multi-agent framework that adaptively creates tools to retrieve information from heterogeneous documents and verify precise conditions in the query. Unlike code-action agents that couple planning and implementation in a single generation step, LangPoli separates a natural-language policy from environment-specific code synthesis. This enables the creation of dynamic tools tailored to each document’s unique structure. Actor agents then convert these verbal action guidelines into executable code to collect observations. A critic agent evaluates the accumulated evidence against the query predicates and provides info-gap feedback to the policy agent, creating a closed loop that enables self-improvement over iterations. We note that concepts such as the plan/action structure Wan et al. (2024) ; Erdogan et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) , code as action instead of predefined sets Wang et al. (2024b) ; Yuan et al. (2024) ; Wölflein et al. (2025) ; Nguyen et al. (2025) , evaluation using LLM agents Shinn et al. (2023) ; Miao et al. (2024) ; Zhuge et al. (2025) ; Yuan and Xie (2025) , and adaptive tool usage Schick et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Wang et al. (2025a) ; Chen et al. (2025) have been established in the field, and LangPoli is a domain-specific adaptation of these components for the underexplored task of scientific data curation. Still, benchmarking LangPoli and other methods on SciCurateBench reveals the difficulty of the task and provides insights into the factors contributing to success.

Figure 1: SciCurateBench promotes adaptive tool creation for efficiently exploring, analyzing, and summarizing heterogeneous scientific files, including manuscripts, supplementary data, and raw datasets. We provide comprehensive benchmarking of popular agentic AI baselines on scientific data curation, including plain LLMs, reasoning agents, tool-using agents, tool-creating agents, and feedback-based agents. Our experiments show that LangPoli is the only method that performs consistently well on both tasks of SciCurateBench, reaching 83.16% F1 on paper classification (vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and 69.43% F1 on structured information retrieval (vs. 59.13% for the strongest baseline). The framework also shows strong performance on public benchmarks of LitSearch Ajith et al. (2024) , BEIR Thakur et al. (2021) , and TREC Craswell et al. (2020) , particularly excelling on long documents where its created tools enable efficient targeted exploration. We show that the tools generated by LangPoli maintain high execution success rates and code maintainability scores while effectively supporting the exploration process. Finally, we explore curriculum transfer, a form of knowledge distillation where successful tool creation sequences are refactored and transferred as structured curricula to accelerate performance on related tasks. This approach enables the system to leverage problem-solving strategies learned from previous curation tasks, further improving efficiency and effectiveness on new scientific data curation problems.

Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scicuratebench-D885/ .

We show that popular LLM reasoning methods achieve only suboptimal performance on the benchmark. To further push performance and study the factors contributing to success, we propose LangPoli, a multi-agent framework that adaptively creates tools to retrieve information from heterogeneous documents and verify precise conditions in the query. Unlike code-action agents that couple planning and implementation in a single generation step, LangPoli separates a natural-language policy from environment-specific code synthesis. This enables the creation of dynamic tools tailored to each document’s unique structure. Actor agents then convert these verbal action guidelines into executable code to collect observations. A critic agent evaluates the accumulated evidence against the query predicates and provides info-gap feedback to the policy agent, creating a closed loop that enables self-improvement over iterations. We note that concepts such as the plan/action structure Wan et al. (2024) ; Erdogan et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) , code as action instead of predefined sets Wang et al. (2024b) ; Yuan et al. (2024) ; Wölflein et al. (2025) ; Nguyen et al. (2025) , evaluation using LLM agents Shinn et al. (2023) ; Miao et al. (2024) ; Zhuge et al. (2025) ; Yuan and Xie (2025) , and adaptive tool usage Schick et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Wang et al. (2025a) ; Chen et al. (2025) have been established in the field, and LangPoli is a domain-specific adaptation of these components for the underexplored task of scientific data curation. Still, benchmarking LangPoli and other methods on SciCurateBench reveals the difficulty of the task and provides insights into the factors contributing to success.

Figure 1: SciCurateBench promotes adaptive tool creation for efficiently exploring, analyzing, and summarizing heterogeneous scientific files, including manuscripts, supplementary data, and raw datasets. We provide comprehensive benchmarking of popular agentic AI baselines on scientific data curation, including plain LLMs, reasoning agents, tool-using agents, tool-creating agents, and feedback-based agents. Our experiments show that LangPoli is the only method that performs consistently well on both tasks of SciCurateBench, reaching 83.16% F1 on paper classification (vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and 69.43% F1 on structured information retrieval (vs. 59.13% for the strongest baseline). The framework also shows strong performance on public benchmarks of LitSearch Ajith et al. (2024) , BEIR Thakur et al. (2021) , and TREC Craswell et al. (2020) , particularly excelling on long documents where its created tools enable efficient targeted exploration. We show that the tools generated by LangPoli maintain high execution success rates and code maintainability scores while effectively supporting the exploration process. Finally, we explore curriculum transfer, a form of knowledge distillation where successful tool creation sequences are refactored and transferred as structured curricula to accelerate performance on related tasks. This approach enables the system to leverage problem-solving strategies learned from previous curation tasks, further improving efficiency and effectiveness on new scientific data curation problems.

passages.text: To validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning 5 for LoRA, we conducted LoRA fine-tuning experiments on natural language generation, image classification, and commonsense reasoning tasks, following the existing LoRA studies [ 21 , 63 , 56 , 41 , 26 ] . All experiments were performed in PyTorch [ 42 ] on a single H100 GPU with 80 GB VRAM. We downloaded the pre-trained models using Hugging Face Transformers library [ 57 ] .

Following [ 21 , 63 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the GPT-2 medium model [ 45 ] on E2E natural language generation challenge task [ 38 ] , which assesses the fine-tuned model’s ability to generate fluent and semantically accurate sentences from meaning representations. We followed the same experimental setup as in [ 63 ] , except that we tuned the learning rate over { 0.02 , 0.04 , … , 0.30 } \{0.02,0.04,\dots,0.30\} for SGD and { 0.0002 , 0.0004 , … , 0.0030 } \{0.0002,0.0004,\dots,0.0030\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query and value matrices of the attention layers in the GPT-2 model. We also fixed the rank to r = 4 r=4 , the scaling factor of B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} to 32 32 , the batch size to 8 8 , the dropout to 0.1 0.1 , and the train epoch to 5 5 with a linear learning-rate schedule. We set the weight decay to 0.01 0.01 for the SGD and AdamW methods. We evaluated all methods by five metrics, BLEU [ 40 ] , NIST [ 12 ] , METEOR [ 3 ] , ROUGE-L [ 27 ] , and CIDEr [ 53 ] , on the test set. To validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically, we investigate how preconditioning affects training time. For this purpose, we compared training times of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning. The experimental setup was the same as that described in Sec. 7.3 . The difference in training times mainly stems from dataset size and the computational cost of preconditioning. Figure 1 shows the results. Each method shows the mean and standard deviation of training times over all learning rates we used for validation. We observed that, although there are some differences due to constant time factors, the results are almost the same across all methods, including the AdamW with our preconditioning 5 as it admits the efficient implementation described in Sec. 5.1 . Consequently, these results validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically and show the computational efficiency of our preconditioning 5 .
